body: An option is a right, not an obligation, to trade something at a fixed price before a fixed date. That is the whole definition. Everything else — the Greeks, the smile, the strategies — is bookkeeping on top of it. Calls and puts A call gives you the right to buy at the strike. You want the price up. A put gives you the right to sell at the strike. You want the price down. Whoever sold you that right has the mirror position and an obligation rather than a choice. This asymmetry is the entire product: the buyer's loss is capped at the premium, and the seller's is not. Move the spot slider on that chart. Below the strike the line is flat — you simply do not exercise, and the premium is gone. Above it the payoff turns and climbs at the same rate as the underlying. The kink sits exactly on the strike, which is why option payoffs are drawn with corners rather than curves. Strike, expiry, premium Three numbers define a contract. Strike — the price you may transact at. Expiry — the date the right lapses. Premium — what the right costs. A contract usually covers 100 shares, so a premium quoted at 3.02 costs £302. The calculator calls this the multiplier, and forgetting it is the most common arithmetic error in option trading. Moneyness An option is in the money if exercising it right now would be worth something, at the money if the strike is roughly spot, and out of the money if exercising would be pointless. A call at a 90 strike with spot at 100 is 10 in the money; the same call with spot at 80 is 10 out of the money and worth only whatever chance remains. Intrinsic and extrinsic value Premium splits cleanly into two parts. Intrinsic value is what the option is worth if it expired this second — max(spot − strike, 0) for a call. It cannot be negative, because you would simply not exercise. Extrinsic value is everything else: the price of the time remaining and the uncertainty in it. It is the entire premium of an out of the money option, and it decays to nothing by expiry with mathematical certainty. That decay is the central fact of being long options. You are paying, every day, for the possibility that you are right. Set the days elapsed slider on the chart above and watch the pre expiry line sag towards the hard expiry line — that gap is extrinsic value draining away. Why the expiry line has corners Look at the two lines on the chart. The solid one is the payoff at expiry: piecewise linear, kinked exactly at the strike, because at expiry an option is worth its intrinsic value and nothing else. The dashed one is the modelled value before expiry, and it is smooth. It sits above the expiry line everywhere, and the distance between them is the extrinsic value you still own. Both lines meet at expiry. Every options strategy is, in some sense, a bet about how those two lines converge. What comes next The Greeks are the four sensitivities that describe how the dashed line moves when something changes — spot, time, or volatility. They are less intimidating than the notation suggests, and they are the subject of the next page.

The Greeks are four questions about the same position, each asking what happens to its value when one thing moves and everything else stands still. You do not need the calculus to use them. You need to know which one is currently your problem. Delta — how much like the underlying is this? Delta is the change in the option's value for a one point move in the underlying. A call runs from 0 (hopelessly out of the money) to 1 (so deep in the money it behaves like stock). A put runs from 0 to −1. The useful reading is as equivalent position size . A 0.4 delta call on 100 shares behaves, for small moves, like owning 40 shares. Sum the deltas across a book and you have your net directional exposure in a single number — which is exactly what a trading desk's risk system reports. Gamma — how fast is delta changing? Gamma is the rate of change of delta. High gamma means your directional exposure is unstable: the position becomes rapidly more long as the price rises and more short as it falls. Gamma is largest at the money and close to expiry. This is why the last day of a contract's life is the dangerous one — a position that was comfortably hedged in the morning can be badly wrong by the afternoon without the underlying doing anything dramatic. Long options are long gamma, which is pleasant: the position gets longer as it wins. Short options are short gamma, which is the opposite, and it is the mechanism by which sold options produce sudden large losses. Theta — what does waiting cost? Theta is the value lost per day from time passing alone. It is negative when you are long options and positive when you are short. Theta and gamma are two sides of one trade. Being long gamma — profiting from movement — is paid for with negative theta. Being short gamma earns theta and sells you the risk. There is no position that is long gamma and long theta; if you think you have found one, check the trade again. Vega — what if the market changes its mind about risk? Vega is the change in value for a one point move in implied volatility. It is not actually a Greek letter, which tells you something about how the vocabulary grew. Vega matters more than most people expect. You can be exactly right about direction and still lose, because implied volatility collapsed after the event you were positioned for. This is routine around earnings: the move happens, and the option holder loses anyway. A straddle is nearly pure vega at the money — flat delta, and its value is almost entirely a view on volatility. Drag the volatility slider and watch the pre expiry line lift and fall while the expiry line stays exactly where it is. That difference is what you are actually trading. Which one kills you In roughly this order: 1. Gamma , because it turns a manageable position into an unmanageable one without warning, and it is worst exactly when you have least time to react. 2. Vega , because it moves against you at the same moment as everything else — volatility rises when markets fall, so a hedge gets more expensive precisely when you want it. 3. Theta , which is at least honest. It takes a predictable amount every day and never surprises anyone. 4. Delta , which is the risk everyone thinks about and the one most easily hedged. The calculator reports all four aggregated across a whole position, which is the only level at which they are useful — individual leg Greeks rarely tell you what you want to know.

Black Scholes takes six inputs: spot, strike, time, rate, carry and volatility. Five of those are observable. Volatility is not — nobody knows what the future holds. So the market inverts the problem. It quotes a price, and you solve backwards for the volatility that price implies. That number is implied volatility , and it is the only genuinely negotiable input. Everything else is arithmetic. Options are quoted in volatility On a professional desk, options are not really priced in currency. They are priced in vol, and the currency figure falls out at the end. Two options on different underlyings at different strikes with different premiums are directly comparable once expressed as implied volatility — which is the whole reason the convention exists. When someone says an option "looks expensive", they almost never mean the premium. They mean the implied volatility is high relative to what they expect the underlying to actually do. Implied versus realised Realised volatility is what the underlying did, measured after the fact. Implied volatility is what the market is charging for it in advance. The gap between them is the trade. Selling options is a bet that implied exceeds realised; buying them is the reverse. Implied is usually a little higher, which is the risk premium option sellers earn — and which is also why selling volatility wins most of the time and occasionally loses catastrophically. Move the volatility slider on that strangle. The expiry line does not budge — at expiry only the spot price matters. But the pre expiry line moves a great deal, because the position's mark to market is a pure volatility view until the last day. Short volatility positions are marked against you long before they are settled against you. The smile Black Scholes assumes one volatility for all strikes. The market disagrees. Plot implied volatility against strike and you get a curve, not a line: out of the money puts trade at higher implied volatility than at the money options, and often higher than out of the money calls. The shape is called the volatility smile , or the skew when it leans one way. It exists because the model's assumptions are wrong in a specific direction. Returns are not normally distributed; crashes are larger and more frequent than the maths allows, and they are correlated with everyone wanting protection at the same time. The smile is the market pricing in what the model leaves out. Equity indices show a pronounced downside skew for exactly this reason. FX tends toward a more symmetric smile, because either currency can be the one that collapses. What this means in practice A single volatility number for a multi strike position, which is what this site's calculator uses, is a simplification. It is fine for understanding shape and wrong for pricing a real trade against a real surface. If you are quoted a price, ask what vol it implies before deciding whether it is expensive. If a strategy looks like free money, you are usually short a tail that is not in the model. The smile exists precisely because those tails are real. I spent a good part of my time at Otkritie building the pricing engine that produced these curves for the desk — implied vol, the smile, and the Greeks that fall out of them, across index, commodity, FX and single stock options. The lesson that stuck: the model is a language for expressing a view, not a source of truth. It is most dangerous when it agrees with you.

The view: Up, and soon enough to beat theta. When it fits You want exposure to a rise without putting up the cash for the shares, and you can name a date by which you expect it. The premium is the most you can lose, which makes this the usual first option anyone buys. What goes wrong Time decay works against you every day, and accelerates as expiry approaches. Being right about direction but late is the same as being wrong. A fall in implied volatility can lose you money even if the underlying rises.

The view: Down, or a hedge against something you own. When it fits Either an outright bearish view, or insurance on a holding you do not want to sell. As a hedge it is expensive precisely when you most want it, because volatility rises as markets fall. What goes wrong Puts are usually priced above their theoretical value, because everyone wants the same insurance. The premium is a certain cost against an uncertain payoff. Time decay again — a slow decline can still lose money.

The view: Flat to mildly up, and you are content to sell at the strike. When it fits You hold the asset, you would be happy selling at a particular level, and you want to be paid for the wait. Popular as an income trade, and reasonable when you genuinely mean the sell. What goes wrong You keep the entire downside and cap the upside — the payoff is the opposite shape to the one people assume they are buying. A sharp rally means you sell at the strike and watch it keep going. The premium is small compensation for a large move in either direction.

The view: You want to own it, but lower. When it fits You are a willing buyer at a price below spot. Selling the put pays you to wait, and if it is assigned you buy at a level you already chose. What goes wrong Identical payoff to a covered call — the downside is the whole move to zero, less the premium. You get assigned exactly when you least want to buy, because the price fell for a reason. The cash is tied up for the life of the trade.

The view: Up, but only so far. When it fits You have a target rather than a hope. Selling the upper strike funds part of the position and cuts the amount time decay can take from you. What goes wrong The cap is real: everything above the short strike belongs to someone else. Both legs have to be closed, so spreads cost more to trade than they look. Maximum profit only arrives at expiry, not on the way there.

The view: Down, to a level you can name. When it fits A bearish view with a floor in mind — support, a valuation, a level you do not expect to break. Cheaper than the outright put for the same reason. What goes wrong Capped at the lower strike, so a crash pays no more than a slide. Still a debit: you can lose the whole premium. Short put legs can be assigned early if they go deep in the money.

The view: Something is about to happen. No idea which way. When it fits Ahead of a binary event — earnings, a ruling, a launch — where the size of the move matters more than its sign. What goes wrong You are buying volatility that is already priced for the event, so the move has to beat expectations, not just happen. Implied volatility usually collapses the moment the news lands, which can lose money even on a correct call. Two premiums to recover means the breakevens are further out than they feel.

The view: Quiet, and quieter than the market is pricing. When it fits When implied volatility looks expensive relative to what you expect to be realised. It wins most of the time, which is exactly what makes it dangerous. What goes wrong Losses are unbounded on the upside and very large on the downside. A high win rate hides the shape: many small gains and occasional catastrophic ones. Margin requirements expand as the position moves against you, forcing you out at the worst moment.

The view: Range bound, and you want to sleep. When it fits The disciplined version of selling volatility. The wings cost part of the premium and convert an unbounded loss into a known one. What goes wrong The maximum loss is usually several times the credit received. Four legs means four lots of spread and commission. It needs the underlying to stay inside the range at expiry, not merely to pass through it.

The view: It pins, right here. When it fits A precise view on where something settles, with very little capital at risk. The payoff peak is sharp and only exists at expiry. What goes wrong The profit zone is narrow and the peak is only reached at expiry. Three strikes, four contracts — execution costs eat a low premium trade. Usually expires worthless, which is the price of the asymmetry.

The view: I want to keep this, but not the tail risk. When it fits A concentrated holding you cannot or will not sell — vested shares being the obvious case. The short call funds the insurance, sometimes entirely. What goes wrong You give up the upside above the call strike, which on a concentrated position is often the whole reason you held it. Selling calls against shares you cannot deliver creates a real problem if assigned. For employee shares, the tax treatment of a collar is rarely as simple as the payoff diagram.

Sell a naked put and your broker asks for a large deposit. Buy a further out of the money put against it, turning the position into a spread with a known worst case, and the requirement collapses. Nothing about your view changed. What changed is that the margin system can now see the hedge. That system, on most futures and options exchanges, is SPAN — Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk, introduced by the CME in 1988 and licensed by exchanges worldwide. It is not complicated, but it is almost never explained, so people learn its behaviour by being surprised by it. The idea Strategy based margining looks at each position and applies a rule. Portfolio margining asks a different question: across a set of plausible market moves, what is the worst this whole portfolio does in one day? That number, roughly, is your margin. Because it values the portfolio as a whole, offsetting positions offset. A long call and a short call at a higher strike are not two margin charges; they are one spread with a capped loss. The risk array The exchange publishes, for each contract, two parameters: a price scan range — how far it thinks the underlying can move in a day — and a volatility scan range . SPAN then revalues your portfolio under sixteen scenarios built from those two numbers. Underlying move Volatility Weight 1–2 Unchanged Up / down 100% 3–4 +⅓ range Up / down 100% 5–6 −⅓ range Up / down 100% 7–8 +⅔ range Up / down 100% 9–10 −⅔ range Up / down 100% 11–12 +1 range Up / down 100% 13–14 −1 range Up / down 100% 15 +2 ranges Unchanged 35% 16 −2 ranges Unchanged 35% Fourteen scenarios walk the price across the scan range in thirds, each paired with volatility rising and falling. The last two are the tail: a move of twice the scan range, counted at a fraction — conventionally 35% — because the exchange wants some charge for a crash without margining every account as though one is due tomorrow. Your scan risk is the worst loss across those sixteen rows. Note what this implies: the volatility legs mean a short option position can be charged its worst case on a day the underlying does not move at all. Drag the volatility slider on that strangle and watch the pre expiry line drop while the expiry line stays put. Rows 1 and 2 of the risk array are exactly that move. This is why short volatility positions get margin calls in quiet markets — the scan found the vol up scenario, not a price move. The parts nobody mentions Scan risk is the headline, but the total is built from four more pieces. Intra commodity spread charge. SPAN treats all months of a contract as one underlying, which is generous — a long March and short June future nets to almost nothing. But the months do not move identically, so a charge is added back for calendar spread risk. It is small, and it surprises people who expected a perfectly hedged spread to be free. Inter commodity spread credit. Related products get a discount for offsetting. Long crude against short heating oil is genuinely less risky than either alone, and the exchange grants a percentage credit for recognised pairs. Delivery or spot month charge. Contracts near expiry behave badly — liquidity thins and squeezes happen — so an extra charge applies as delivery approaches. Short option minimum. The one that catches people. A portfolio of deep out of the money short options can scan to almost no risk, because in all sixteen scenarios the options stay worthless. SPAN refuses to believe this and imposes a floor per short contract. Sell enough far out of the money options and your margin is set entirely by this minimum, with the scan irrelevant. The total is roughly: What this means when you trade Defining your risk cuts your margin, often dramatically. Buying the wing on a short position costs premium and buys back a large part of the deposit. This is most of the reason iron condors exist rather than strangles. Margin is not static. The exchange raises scan ranges when realised volatility rises — which is precisely when your position is already losing. Requirements expand into a falling market, and forced liquidation is a liquidity event, not a solvency one. That mechanism has ended more accounts than bad directional calls. Check the short option minimum before scaling. A strategy that looks capital efficient at ten contracts may be floored at a hundred. Your broker may add to it. SPAN is the exchange's number. Brokers routinely apply a multiplier on top, and retail multipliers can be substantial. Notes from building one I built the risk and margin engine at Otkritie — SPAN portfolio margining across futures and options on index, commodity, FX and single stocks, feeding a real time engine handling over a million updates a second for 400,000 investors. Three things I did not expect going in. The arithmetic is the easy part. Sixteen revaluations per contract is nothing. The hard part is the reference data : scan ranges, tiers, spread definitions and credit rates change, they arrive as files on a schedule, and a stale parameter produces a confidently wrong number rather than an error. The second is that the option pricing model inside the margin calculation has to match the one on the trading screen , or clients see a margin requirement that disagrees with their own P&L and — reasonably — do not trust either. The third is that margin is a real time obligation, not a report . It has to be right on every tick, because it gates whether an order can be placed at all. That constraint, more than the mathematics, is what makes a margin engine an engineering problem. Beyond SPAN Exchanges are migrating from the original algorithm to SPAN 2 , which combines a historical value at risk model with a stress component and handles liquidity and concentration more explicitly. The intuition above still holds — scenarios, portfolio offsets, and add ons for the things a scenario grid misses. The parameters change; the shape of the answer does not. For the authoritative detail, go to the exchange's own methodology documentation rather than a textbook. It is free, precise, and updated when the rules change.

Value at Risk answers one question: over some horizon, at some confidence, how much could I lose? A 1 day 99% VAR of £1m means that on 99 days out of 100 you expect to lose less than £1m. It says nothing whatsoever about the hundredth day, and that omission is the entire debate. Three ways to compute it Historical simulation. Take the last few hundred days of market moves, apply each one to today's portfolio, sort the resulting P&Ls, and read off the percentile. No distributional assumption, which is its great virtue. Its great weakness is that it can only produce a crisis it has already seen — a two year window that contains no crash will price no crash. Variance–covariance. Assume returns are normally distributed, compute the portfolio's volatility from a covariance matrix, and multiply by the appropriate z score. Fast, analytic, and wrong in a specific direction: financial returns have fatter tails than the normal distribution, so this method systematically understates exactly the losses you built it to measure. It also handles options badly, because a linear approximation of a convex payoff breaks down at the sizes that matter. Monte Carlo. Simulate many paths from a model, revalue the portfolio under each, take the percentile. Flexible and the only practical choice for genuinely non linear books. Expensive, and no more truthful than the model generating the paths. Scaling, and a common misuse A 1 day VAR is often scaled to ten days by multiplying by √10. That step assumes returns are independent and identically distributed. They are not: volatility clusters, and bad days arrive in runs. Square root of time scaling therefore understates multi day risk precisely during the episodes it is supposed to capture. Why VAR is not a coherent risk measure There is a formal definition of what a sensible risk measure should do, set out by Artzner and co authors. One requirement is subadditivity : combining two portfolios should never produce more risk than the sum of their parts, because diversification cannot be harmful. VAR fails this. It is possible to construct two positions whose combined VAR exceeds the sum of the individual VARs — typically involving discrete, low probability large losses that individually sit just outside the confidence threshold and together fall inside it. A risk measure that can penalise diversification is not merely inelegant; it creates an incentive to concentrate. VAR has a second, more everyday failure. It is a threshold , so it is blind to everything past it. Two portfolios can have identical 99% VAR while one loses £1.1m on the worst day and the other loses £90m. Selling far out of the money options is the classic way to report a flattering VAR while accumulating precisely the risk the number cannot see. Expected Shortfall Expected Shortfall — also called CVaR or conditional VAR — is the average loss given that you are in the tail beyond the VAR threshold. VAR asks how bad things get before the worst 1%. ES asks how bad the worst 1% actually is. ES is subadditive and coherent. It cannot be gamed by pushing risk just past a percentile, because it integrates over everything out there. This is why the Basel Committee's Fundamental Review of the Trading Book replaced 99% VAR with 97.5% Expected Shortfall for market risk capital. The confidence level dropped because, for a normal distribution, 97.5% ES lands close to 99% VAR — so the change alters what is measured more than how much capital results. The catch with ES ES is harder to backtest. VAR backtesting is simple: count the days the loss exceeded the forecast. At 99% over 250 days you expect around two or three exceptions, and Basel's traffic light framework escalates as the count rises — a straightforward, auditable test. ES has no equivalent clean test, because it is a conditional average rather than a threshold. Verifying it needs indirect approaches, and this is a live practical problem rather than a theoretical footnote: a number you cannot readily validate is a number that can drift. What both miss Neither measure covers the risks that actually close firms. Liquidity. Both assume you can exit at the marked price. In a crisis you cannot, and the mark is the first thing to become fictional. Correlation breakdown. Diversification is priced from history. Correlations converge towards one in a crash, exactly when the model is relying on them not to. Funding. Losing money and being unable to meet a margin call are different failures. The second is what forces liquidation, and it does not appear in either measure. LTCM had a sophisticated risk framework. What ended it was a correlated move in positions assumed independent, met by margin calls that could not be funded. The mathematics was not the weak point. Building one At Revolut I owned the greenfield risk system behind the wealth and trading platform — mark to market, collateral and variation margin, VAR and Expected Shortfall, DV01, Greeks, book value and accruals, across fixed income, FX and interest rate derivatives, spot FX, crypto and commodities. The lesson that transferred to everything since: the number is the easy part, and the data lineage is the whole job. A VAR figure is only as good as the position feed, the price history and the corporate action handling underneath it. Most of what looked like model risk turned out, on inspection, to be a stale price or a position that had been booked twice. The second lesson is that a risk number nobody can explain gets ignored. If a trader cannot see which position drove the move, the report becomes decoration. Attribution — being able to decompose the number back to its causes — matters more for whether a risk system changes behaviour than the sophistication of the model producing it.

Equity desks talk in delta. Rates desks talk in DV01 — the dollar value of a basis point. It is the change in a position's value when the relevant yield moves by one hundredth of a percent. That is all it is. A bond with a DV01 of £850 gains roughly £850 if yields fall one basis point, and loses roughly £850 if they rise one. You will also see it as PV01 or BPV ; for most purposes the distinction is not worth arguing about. Why a basis point Because it makes unlike things comparable. A ten year gilt, an interest rate swap, a futures contract and a portfolio of all three have no common unit until you express each as sensitivity to the same small move. Once you do, you can add them up, and the sum is the position. This is the practical reason DV01 wins over duration on a trading desk. Duration is a percentage, so it needs a notional and a price before it means anything. DV01 is already in money. The relationship to duration They are the same idea in different clothing: A £10m position with modified duration 8 and a price of par has a DV01 of roughly £8,000. Duration tells you the percentage sensitivity; DV01 tells you the cash. Risk systems report the cash, because that is what a limit is denominated in. Convexity, and the direction of the error DV01 is a first derivative — a straight line approximation to a curved relationship. For a plain bond, the price/yield curve bends favourably: convexity is positive, so prices rise more than DV01 predicts when yields fall, and fall less than it predicts when they rise. For a one basis point move that error is negligible, which is why the unit is one basis point. For a fifty basis point move it is not, and a DV01 only view understates your position in a rally and overstates the damage in a sell off. Not everything is positively convex. Mortgage backed securities and callable bonds can exhibit negative convexity — as yields fall, borrowers refinance and the expected life shortens, so the position stops rallying. Here DV01 is not merely imprecise; it points the wrong way about what happens next. Anything with an embedded option needs the second order term. One number is not enough DV01 as usually quoted assumes a parallel shift — every point on the curve moves by the same basis point. Curves do not oblige. They steepen, flatten and twist, and a portfolio can be flat on parallel DV01 while carrying a large bet on the shape. Consider a book that is long two year and short ten year in DV01 neutral size. Total DV01: zero. A parallel move does nothing. A steepening move can cost a great deal. The fix is key rate , or partial, DV01: bucket the curve by tenor and shift each bucket separately, holding the rest fixed. You get a vector rather than a scalar — sensitivity at 2y, 5y, 10y, 30y — which is what a rates risk report actually shows. The scalar is the sum, and the sum is the least informative row. Hedging with it DV01 is how hedge ratios are set. To hedge a position with an instrument, you match the DV01s: If a corporate bond position has a DV01 of £42,000 and a futures contract has a DV01 of £70 per contract, you need about 600 contracts. In practice this is adjusted for the basis between the two instruments and rebalanced as DV01 itself drifts with yields — the hedge ratio is not constant, which is convexity appearing again. Where it sits in a risk stack DV01 is a sensitivity , not a loss estimate. It tells you how exposed you are per unit of move; it does not tell you how large a move to expect. That is the job of VAR and Expected Shortfall, which combine sensitivities with a view on distribution. Both matter, and they fail differently. Sensitivities are precise and local: correct for small moves, silent about large ones. Distributional measures cover the large moves and depend entirely on the history or model you feed them. A desk watches both, and trusts neither alone. From the build side My first serious risk work was extending Deutsche Bank's FX desk risk calculator to Fixed Income — taking a system that priced one asset class and teaching it another, then migrating the workflow off spreadsheets onto a live platform. Later, at Revolut, DV01 was one line in a greenfield engine that also carried mark to market, collateral and variation margin, VAR/ES and Greeks. The recurring difficulty was never the derivative. It was agreeing what a position was : the same trade represented differently in three systems, settlement conventions that shifted a cash flow by a day, and day count conventions that quietly changed the answer. Anyone who has built one of these will tell you the same thing — the risk number is a thin layer of arithmetic over a deep pile of reference data, and the pile is where the bugs live.

Every other page here describes a position and what it is worth. This one is about what happens next, because an option is not a bet you place and leave. Sell one and you have taken on an exposure that changes every time the underlying moves, and the only way to see what that costs is to run it forward. What the premium actually buys Sell a thirty day at the money call at 25% volatility and roughly 300 lands in your account. It is tempting to read that as income. It is not. It is the market's estimate of what it will cost you to stay flat until expiry. Being short the call leaves you short delta as the underlying rises, so you buy to stay hedged. When it falls you sell. Buy high, sell low, thirty times, and the losses accumulate — that is what being short gamma means, and it is the only reason anyone pays you the premium in the first place. Run the figure above a few times. The premium is always about 300. The cost of hedging is always about 300. What is left over changes sign from path to path and is small either way. That is not the hedge failing. That is the option being correctly priced. When you keep it The premium is the price of a forecast: 25% annualised. The market either delivers that or it does not. The underlying barely leaves a six point range, the hedge rarely has to chase it, and the hedging bill comes to about 180 against the 300 you took in. You keep the difference. This is the entire business model of a short volatility book, and it is also why those books look brilliant for long stretches and then do not. Same position, same discipline, same 300 collected. The underlying travels to 125 instead of 106, the hedge has to chase every swing, and the hedging bill comes to nearly 380 — the premium gone, and about 75 of your own money with it. The asymmetry worth noticing is not in these three numbers, which are close to symmetric around the break even. It is in the distribution behind them. Realised volatility cannot fall below zero, so the best case is bounded: you keep the premium and no more. There is no matching ceiling on the other side. The quiet path pays you a known maximum; the violent path has no maximum at all, and a thirty day chart of a market that merely doubled its volatility is nowhere near the bad end of that distribution. The part the model does not tell you Black Scholes assumes you rebalance continuously. Nobody does. Hedge thirty times instead of infinitely often and you are left with an error that has nothing to do with whether your volatility forecast was right — it is the residual of a discrete approximation to a continuous instruction. That error shrinks as you hedge more often, roughly with the square root of the number of rebalances. Going from six hedges to sixty cuts the spread of outcomes by about two thirds. It also multiplies your transaction costs, which the model prices at zero and your broker does not. So the real question on a hedging desk is never "how do I eliminate this error". It is "where does the marginal hedge stop paying for itself" — and that is a question about spread, commission and market impact, not about the Greeks. Why this page exists The risk systems I have spent most of my career on exist to answer this question across a book rather than a single position: what am I short, what will it cost me to stay flat, and what happens to that number if the world moves. SPAN answers a version of it for margin. VAR answers a version of it for capital. This is the version a trader lives with every day. The figures above use the same Black Scholes implementation as the options P&L calculator — no separate demo model, and no market data. The paths are generated and seeded, so the same button always produces the same story.

A price on a screen looks like a fact about now. It is a claim about the past, made by a venue, carried through several systems that each changed it a little, and displayed some milliseconds — or seconds — after the event it describes. Every system that prices, margins or executes against that number inherits those changes, whether or not anyone wrote them down. Market data is the least glamorous part of a trading platform and the one most likely to be quietly wrong. Pricing models get reviewed. Feed handlers mostly get noticed when they stop. What actually arrives Venues publish at different depths, and the depth decides what you can know. Level What it carries What it lets you answer L1 Best bid, best offer, last trade Where is the market? L2 Aggregated size at each price level How much can I trade before the price moves? L3 Every individual order, add / modify / cancel Who is queued ahead of me, and is that size real? Most retail facing systems run on L1 and a few levels of L2. That is enough to show a price, and not enough to know what a large order will cost — which is why execution systems and display systems often subscribe to the same instrument at different depths. The other distinction that matters is snapshot versus incremental . A snapshot is the whole book; an incremental feed is a stream of changes to it. Incremental feeds are smaller and faster, and they carry a sequence number for a reason: apply one update out of order, or miss one, and every book you build afterwards is wrong in a way that looks perfectly plausible. Normalisation is where meaning changes Each venue has its own symbology, tick sizes, lot sizes, price multipliers, trading calendars and conventions for what a "trade" is. A feed handler translates all of that into one internal model, and every translation is a decision someone made once and nobody revisits: Instrument identity. The same economic thing can be several listings, and one ticker can mean different things on different venues. Mapping errors here do not crash anything; they price one instrument off another. Price scaling. Pence versus pounds, quoted versus clean price, a futures multiplier applied twice or not at all. A factor of 100 is easy to spot. A factor of 1.0125 is not. Trade conditions. Auction prints, off book trades, late reports and corrections all arrive as "trades". A last price field that includes them is measuring something different from one that does not. Calendars. Half days, holidays and session breaks decide whether a quiet feed is a closed market or a broken connection. The useful habit is to keep the raw message alongside the normalised one for long enough to answer "what did the venue actually say?" When a client disputes a fill, that question arrives within the hour. Gaps, recovery and the book you cannot trust Sequence numbers make gaps detectable; they do not make them harmless. When a gap appears the honest state of the book is unknown , and the system has to choose: 1. Stop and recover. Mark the instrument stale, request a snapshot or replay, rebuild, then resume. Correct, and briefly blind. 2. Carry on. Keep applying updates to a book known to be missing some. Fast, and wrong in a way that cannot be measured. Anything that prices or margins should take the first option and say so. The second is how a crossed book — best bid above best offer — ends up feeding a risk engine, which then reports a profit that does not exist. Crossed and locked markets are worth checking for explicitly. They are rare on a single healthy venue, common across venues for a few milliseconds, and almost always a sign of a stale side when they persist. Conflation and staleness A busy instrument can update tens of thousands of times a second, and most consumers cannot use that. Conflation keeps the latest state and drops the intermediate ones: a screen redrawing at 4Hz needs the price as of now, not every price since the last frame. Conflation is right for display and dangerous for anything that needs the path — a stop that should have triggered at a price the conflated stream never showed, or a volume weighted calculation computed over a sample instead of the trades. Staleness is the mirror problem: a price that has not changed may be a quiet market or a dead connection. The two look identical in the data. Good systems carry the time of the last update next to every price, and the age of that timestamp — not the price — is what a dealer looks at first when something seems off. A coloured "seconds since last update" next to a figure is one of the most useful pieces of UI in a dealing tool, because it answers the question before it is asked. Timestamps, plural A single tick can carry several times: when the venue matched or published it; when it reached your network; when your handler decoded it; when your application acted on it. The gaps between them are your latency budget, measured. Keeping only the last one — usually the local receive time — throws away the ability to say whether a slow fill was the venue, the network or your own code. Clocks also need to agree: a timestamp from a server that has drifted by a few milliseconds will make causality appear to run backwards in your logs. What a composite price hides Platforms that quote one price per instrument usually build it from several sources: venues, liquidity providers, a reference feed. The composite is a policy, not a measurement. It has to decide which sources count, how to weight them, how to treat one that has gone quiet, and what to do when they disagree. That policy is invisible in the output. A smooth composite can hide one source that has been stale for a minute and another that has started printing outliers. The defence is to keep each source's contribution inspectable — which source set the bid, how old it was, how far the others were from it — so that when the composite moves, someone can say why. The short version Treat every price as price, source, time — never price alone. Prefer a stale flag to a confident wrong number. Recover from gaps; do not paper over them. Conflate for people, not for risk. Keep the raw message long enough to answer a dispute. None of this is visible when it works, which is exactly why it needs owning. The execution note picks up where the price ends and an order begins, and the market making note covers what a dealer does with the price once it is trusted.

A market maker quotes a price to buy and a price to sell, and earns the gap between them. Described like that it sounds like a toll booth. In practice the spread is the smaller part of the job. The larger part is the inventory that every fill leaves behind, and the uncomfortable fact that the clients most eager to trade with you are often the ones who know something you do not. Where a spread comes from The classic decomposition has three parts, and each points at a different lever: Component What it pays for What moves it Order processing Fees, infrastructure, people Scale and automation Inventory Carrying a position you did not choose Volatility, position size, time to unwind Adverse selection Trading against better informed flow Who the counterparty is, and how fast prices move after the fill Ho and Stoll formalised the inventory part in 1981; Glosten and Milgrom the adverse selection part in 1985. Neither is new. What changes in a real system is that all three are measured continuously, per instrument and per client segment, rather than assumed. Skew before you widen When a market maker accumulates a long position the instinct is to widen both sides. That is usually the wrong move. Widening makes you less competitive on the side that would reduce your risk as well as on the side that would add to it. The better move is to skew : shift both quotes down, so your offer becomes more attractive — someone buys your inventory from you — and your bid less attractive, so fewer people sell you more. The spread can stay the same width while its centre moves away from the market mid. Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008) made this precise. Their reservation price — the price at which the market maker is indifferent to holding one more unit — is the mid adjusted for inventory: where s is the mid, q the signed inventory, γ risk aversion, σ the volatility and T − t the time left to carry the position. Quotes are then placed around r , not around s . A worked illustration, with round numbers rather than market ones: mid 100.00, long 10 units, γ = 0.01 , σ = 2 per square root day, half a day left. The adjustment is 10 × 0.01 × 4 × 0.5 = 0.20 , so the reservation price is 99.80 and both quotes slide twenty cents down. Double the position and the skew doubles. Double the volatility and it quadruples — which is the formula's way of saying that inventory in a fast market is much more expensive than the same inventory in a slow one. The same paper gives the optimal total spread: where k measures how quickly the chance of a fill falls away with distance from the mid. The spread widens with volatility and with the time left to carry the position, and narrows as k rises — when competition for flow is fierce, quoting wide simply stops getting filled. Risk aversion is less obvious than it looks: it raises the first term and lowers the second, so a more cautious market maker skews harder but does not necessarily quote wider. Adverse selection, measured You cannot see a counterparty's information. You can see what the market did after you traded with them. That is a markout : the move in the mid, from your side of the trade, at a set horizon after the fill. Buy at 99.98, mid is 99.90 a second later: −8 ticks at one second. The same at ten seconds and sixty seconds gives a curve. Average those curves by client segment, venue or order type, and the toxic flow identifies itself. Benign flow has markouts that hover around zero. Informed flow has markouts that fall steadily against you, and the horizon at which they stop falling tells you how fast the information was. Markouts are the single most useful number a dealing desk computes, because they turn an argument ("this client is too smart for us") into a measurement, and because they separate two problems that look the same in P&L: quoting too tight, and quoting the wrong people. Hold, net or hedge Every fill leaves exposure, and there are three things to do with it: 1. Hold it and let the skew work it off. Cheapest, if the market cooperates. 2. Net it against opposing client flow. A dealer facing many clients often finds that buyers and sellers offset each other for much of the day, and only the residual needs managing. 3. Hedge it externally — in the underlying, a future, or a correlated instrument. This costs a spread and carries basis risk, but caps the loss. The decision is a limit structure, not a judgement call made trade by trade: position limits per instrument and per correlated group, a loss limit, and rules for when the residual is hedged automatically. A hedging algorithm then decides how — slicing the hedge, choosing venues and managing its own market impact — which is the problem the execution note covers. Options make it two dimensional An options market maker carries the same problem with more axes. The inventory is not a quantity but a set of Greeks: delta, which is hedged continuously in the underlying, and gamma and vega, which can only be reduced by trading other options. Skew then applies to the volatility surface rather than to a price: a book that is long vega lowers the implied volatility it quotes, across the strikes and expiries where it is long. The cost of carrying that gamma is exactly what the dynamic hedging note simulates: the premium collected for an option is the price of the hedging it is about to require. What breaks in practice Stale inputs. Quoting off a price that has stopped updating is the fastest way to be picked off. Every quoting engine needs a staleness kill switch — see the market data note. Correlated inventory. Ten small positions in instruments that move together are one large position. Limits set per instrument miss it. Feedback loops. Your own hedging moves the market your quotes are built on. A hedge that is too aggressive shows up as worse markouts on your own next fills. Regime change. Parameters fitted on a quiet month are wrong on the day it stops being quiet, which is the day they matter. None of this needs exotic maths. It needs every number — spread, skew, markout, residual — to be visible to the people accountable for the book, live, with the age of the data beside it.

"Buy 1,000" is an instruction. What the client receives is a set of fills at prices, times and venues, and the difference between the two is execution. Most of the work happens in the few milliseconds nobody sees, and the quality of it only becomes visible in aggregate — which is why it is measured badly so often. Order types are risk choices Every order type trades certainty of execution against certainty of price. Order Guarantees Risks Market It fills (if there is liquidity) The price, in a thin or fast market Limit The worst price That it never fills Stop That it triggers at a level The fill price after triggering — a stop becomes a market order Stop limit Trigger and worst price Triggering, then not filling, while the market runs away IOC / FOK No resting order left behind Partial or no fill The useful framing for clients and for product teams alike: a market order buys certainty that you trade and pays for it in price; a limit order buys certainty of price and pays for it in the risk of missing the trade. A stop is not protection against gaps — when the market opens through it, the fill is wherever the market is. Smart order routing When the same instrument trades in several places, an order has to decide where to go. A smart order router takes the parent order and the current state of each venue and produces child orders: 1. Build the consolidated book from each venue's depth. 2. Adjust each venue's prices for its fees, rebates and expected fill probability — the headline price is not the price you get. 3. Walk the book, taking the best effective prices until the order is filled or the limit is reached. 4. Send the child orders, ideally so that they arrive together, because the first fill is a signal to anyone watching the other venues. 5. Handle what comes back: partial fills, rejects, and quotes that had moved by the time the order arrived. Step 4 is where latency stops being an engineering metric and becomes a cost. Orders that arrive at different venues a few milliseconds apart give faster participants time to adjust the quotes the router was relying on. Liquidity aggregation A broker or dealer that hedges through several liquidity providers runs the same logic in a different setting. Each provider streams quotes, often with different sizes, different validity, and different rules about whether a request at that price will actually be honoured. Last look — a provider's right to reject a trade request within a short window after seeing it — means a quote is an offer to consider, not a commitment. The aggregator therefore keeps statistics, not just prices: per provider, the fill ratio, the reject ratio by market condition, how long the last look takes, and the markouts after the fill. A provider with the best headline price and a high reject rate in fast markets is often the most expensive one in the book. At Revolut the liquidity aggregation, smart order routing and hedging algorithms ran with a roundtrip under 60 milliseconds. The number matters less than the discipline behind it: knowing where each millisecond went. The latency budget End to end latency is a sum, and each term has an owner: market data in: venue → network → feed handler → book; decision: risk checks, pricing, routing logic; order out: gateway → network → venue; acknowledgement and fill back, through the same path. Measuring only the total tells you there is a problem and nothing about where. Timestamping at each boundary — and keeping the clocks that write those timestamps in agreement — turns "the platform is slow" into "the risk check added 4 milliseconds after the last release", which is a problem someone can fix. Tail latency matters more than the average. A system that answers in 2 milliseconds at the median and 400 at the 99.9th percentile will hurt clients precisely on the busy days, because the tail is where the volume is. Pre trade risk checks Every order passes through checks before it leaves: does the client have the margin, is the size inside limits, is the price within a band of the market, is this order a duplicate, is the instrument tradable right now. They are the cheapest insurance a platform buys, and they sit directly in the latency path, so two properties matter: They must be fast and deterministic — no network calls on the hot path that can stall. They must fail closed. If a check cannot decide, the order does not go. A risk check that times out and lets the order through is not a risk check. Fat finger price bands deserve particular care: too tight and they reject legitimate orders on volatile days, too loose and they let through the error they exist to stop. Measuring what it cost Execution quality is measured against a benchmark, and the choice of benchmark decides the answer. Arrival price. The mid when the order was decided. The gap to the average fill price is implementation shortfall : everything execution cost, including the market moving while you worked the order. Spread capture. Where inside the bid offer the fill landed. VWAP. Fill price against the volume weighted average over the period. Useful for large orders worked over time; flattering for small ones, which are part of the volume they are measured against. Markouts. The same post trade measure a market maker uses, from the client's side: did the price keep moving after the fill? Regulation in Europe frames all of this as best execution: firms must take all sufficient steps to obtain the best possible result for clients, considering price, costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size and nature. The practical consequence is that every one of the numbers above has to be computable after the fact, per order, with the market data that was true at the time — which takes us back to market data. The short version Pick order types for the risk you would rather carry. Route on effective prices, not headline ones. Score liquidity providers on fills and markouts, not quotes. Budget latency per hop, and watch the tail. Keep pre trade checks fast, deterministic and closed on failure. Measure against arrival price before anything that flatters you.

When an agent does something useful, the model gets the credit. When it does something stupid, the model gets the blame. Both are mostly misattributed. The same model is excellent or useless depending on what it is shown, what it is allowed to do, and what happens to its output before anyone relies on it — and all three of those belong to the harness , not the model. A harness is everything wrapped around the model call: context assembly, tools, permissions, hooks, memory and verification. It is ordinary software, it is where most of the engineering effort goes, and it is where a team's taste and standards actually live. The parts Part Question it answers Fails as Context What does the model know right now? Confident answers about the wrong version of the code Tools What can it do? Workarounds through whatever tool is available Permissions What may it do without asking? Either constant interruptions or an incident Hooks What always happens around an action? Rules that are only followed when remembered Memory What carries over between sessions? The same correction made every week Verification How do we know it worked? "Done" meaning "I wrote some code" Context is a budget, not a dump The cheapest way to improve an agent is to give it less, better context. A model reading forty files to find the three that matter is slower, more expensive and more likely to latch onto the wrong pattern than one that is handed the three. What works in practice is layered, scoped context : A short brief at the root of each repository — what the system is for, the hard rules, the commands that prove something works. On this site that is a single AGENTS.md , with CLAUDE.md pointing at it so the two cannot drift. Rules that attach by path. In the workspace I build SHIP in — eight repositories: app, backend, CLI, browser extension, MCP server, website, policies and infrastructure — each repository's conventions live in a rule file that only loads when the agent touches files matching its glob. The backend rules never cost tokens during a front end change. Skills for repeatable procedures — "create a database migration", "regenerate the API client", "prepare a release" — written once, loaded on demand. The test for anything in the brief is whether it is recoverable from the code. Directory structure is; why a choice that looks wrong is deliberate is not. Briefs that describe the code go stale; briefs that record judgement stay useful. Tools shape behaviour An agent uses the tools it has. Give it only a shell and it will edit files with sed , query databases by piping SQL strings and parse JSON with grep . Each works until it does not. Dedicated tools — edit a file by exact replacement, query with a typed interface, read a page as text — make the right action the easy one, and they make actions auditable because their arguments are structured. The same applies to the interfaces an agent reaches outside the machine. A typed MCP server with a narrow set of tools is a contract: what the agent can read, what it can write, and in what shape. That is a much smaller surface to reason about than "it has an API key". Permissions follow reversibility Permission design gets easier once actions are sorted by how hard they are to undo: 1. Read anything in scope — no prompt. 2. Edit the working tree — no prompt, because version control is the undo. 3. Run commands that change local state — allow listed by pattern. 4. Anything outward facing or irreversible — pushing, deploying, sending a message, deleting data, spending money — a human confirms, every time. The failure mode at one end is an agent that asks before every file read and gets switched to "allow everything" by Friday. At the other end it is an agent that force pushes over a colleague's branch. Sorting by reversibility gives a policy people keep. Hooks make rules unforgettable A rule in a prompt is followed when the model remembers it. A hook is followed every time. Anything that must always happen belongs in a hook: A pre tool hook in the SHIP workspace scans every write for secret like patterns and warns before the content lands on disk. An editor hook reminds that a change to the database schema file needs a migration revision — the mistake that is cheapest to catch at edit time and most expensive in production. Formatting and linting after edits, so the diff a reviewer sees is the substance and not the whitespace. The pattern is the same as in any engineering system: move a check from "someone should remember" to "the system does it". Verification is the product The hardest part of agentic work is not producing a change. It is knowing whether the change is right. A harness earns its keep by making verification cheap and non negotiable: a single command that runs the gate — on this site npm run verify , which runs eight numeric suites and a render smoke test, around 330 checks; tests that assert properties rather than snapshots, so the agent cannot pass them by regenerating the expected output; a real environment to look at — a dev server, a browser, a simulator — so "it compiles" is not mistaken for "it works". An agent that can run the gate itself iterates until it passes. An agent that cannot will report success on the first attempt that looks plausible. The agentic workflows note is about building that loop deliberately. Why this is the product Two teams on the same model will get very different results, and the difference is almost entirely harness: what they wrote down, what they automated, what they refuse to let through. That is good news. Models change every few months; a well built harness carries over, and it compounds — every correction written into a rule, a skill or a hook is one the team never makes again.

Every agentic workflow is a loop: decide what to do, do it, check whether it worked, repeat. The first two steps get the demos. The third decides whether the result can be trusted, and it is the one most often left to the model's own judgement — which is to say, skipped. The rule that makes these loops hold up is simple to state: the check has to be something the model cannot talk its way past. Plan, act, verify Plan is where scope gets decided, and where most expensive mistakes are made cheaply. A plan written down before any change — which files, which approach, how success will be shown — gives a human one place to say "no, not like that" before an hour of work goes in the wrong direction. It also gives the agent something to check itself against later. Act should be small. A diff a reviewer can read in two minutes gets read; a diff that touches forty files gets approved. Small steps also make failure cheap: when step four breaks something, steps one to three are still good. Verify is a gate, not an opinion. Compare: Weak check Strong check "The code looks correct" The tests pass The tests the agent just wrote pass Tests that existed before the change still pass Snapshot tests regenerated Property tests: monotonicity, round trips, known answers "It builds" The page renders and the number on it is right The agent says it is done A command exits zero The strong column has one thing in common: the agent does not control the outcome. That is the point. Property checks beat examples For anything that computes, the most robust gate is a set of properties rather than a list of expected outputs. This site's calculators are checked that way: Closed form anchors. Hedging an option at zero volatility must compound to exactly exp(rt) . Round trips. Price at a volatility, invert the price, recover the volatility to 1e 7. Monotonicity. Every lever must pull the right way — more contribution, more money. Statistical tolerance. A Monte Carlo result is compared against its own standard error, not a magic number. Hostile input. An empty field, a crossed market, a quote below intrinsic. An agent can make an example test pass by changing the example. It cannot make "inverting the price recovers the volatility" pass without the maths being right. That asymmetry is what lets a loop run unattended for longer. Humans at the irreversible step Autonomy should scale with reversibility, not with confidence. An agent can iterate on a working tree all afternoon because version control undoes anything. It should not push, deploy, send, delete or pay without a person saying yes — and that approval should be specific to the action, not a blanket "go ahead" that silently covers the next one. On this site the split is explicit: the agent can change anything in the source and run every check, but nothing is live until the static build is regenerated and committed, and that step is mine. Sub agents for separation, not speed Splitting work across agents is tempting for throughput. Its better use is separation of concerns : a reviewer agent that sees only the diff and the brief, not the reasoning that produced it, so it is not persuaded by the author's story; a researcher that reads widely and returns a conclusion, so the main context is not filled with forty files it will never need again; specialists with narrow briefs — security, database migrations, compliance language — whose instructions would be noise in every other task. Each spawn starts cold and re derives context, so it is not free. Use it where independence is the value. Evals: the regression suite for behaviour Code has tests; agent behaviour needs evals — a fixed set of tasks with a way of scoring the result, run whenever the prompt, the tools or the model change. Without them every change to the harness is a guess, and model upgrades become anxious events instead of routine ones. Good evals look like the work: real tasks from the backlog, real failure cases that were fixed once, graded on whether the outcome was correct rather than whether the transcript looked confident. A handful of honest evals beats a leaderboard of synthetic ones. Cost and latency are design inputs Every loop iteration costs tokens and time. That shapes design: give the agent the cheapest check first — the type checker before the full test suite, the unit test before the browser; keep stable context stable, so it can be cached rather than re sent; stop loops that are not converging. Three failed attempts at the same fix usually mean the plan is wrong, not the code. What changes for the team The bottleneck moves. Writing the change gets cheap; specifying it and checking it do not. Teams that do well with agents write better briefs, invest in faster and stricter gates, and treat every recurring correction as a bug in the harness rather than in the model. The harness note covers where those corrections live, and the product engineering note what it does to how a team is organised.

The usual way to give a model knowledge is to put the documents in a vector store and retrieve the closest chunks at question time. It demos well, and it fails quietly — not with an error, but with a fluent answer built from the wrong paragraph of the wrong version of the right document. That failure is structural, and fixing it is less about better retrieval than about deciding what the knowledge actually is. How retrieval goes wrong A retrieval pipeline has four stages, and each loses something: Stage What it does What it loses Chunk Split documents into passages The sentence before, which said "this was rejected" Embed Turn passages into vectors Exact terms — ticker symbols, error codes, names Retrieve Return the nearest passages Anything phrased differently from the question Generate Answer from what came back The fact that what came back was incomplete The last row is the dangerous one. The model cannot know what retrieval did not return, so it answers from what it has, confidently. A decision that was made in March and reversed in May is two documents; whichever chunk is closer to the question wins. Hybrid search fixes recall Semantic search is good at meaning and bad at precise terms. Full text search is the opposite. Running both and merging the results — then re ranking the merged list — fixes most recall problems at modest cost. The AI retrieval stack I built at Nevis combined full text and semantic search for exactly that reason: in wealth management the questions name specific funds, forms and account types, and an embedding alone will happily return a passage about a similar one. Hybrid search makes retrieval better. It does not make it right , because the underlying problem is not finding passages. It is that passages are the wrong unit for most of what an organisation needs to know. Typed knowledge Ask what an engineering team actually needs an agent to know, and the answer is rarely "the paragraph that mentions X". It is: what the team is trying to achieve — goals ; what was decided, by whom, and why — decisions ; what exists — artefacts : services, repositories, documents, pull requests; how those relate — this decision serves that goal, this artefact implements that decision. Represented as typed nodes with typed edges, those questions stop being retrieval problems. "What is the current decision on the auth provider?" is a lookup of a node of type decision , scoped to auth , that has not been superseded — not a similarity search over every message that mentions auth. This is the design behind SHIP: goals, decisions and artefacts as typed nodes instead of prose, which agents read and write through MCP. Provenance and supersession Two properties make a knowledge base trustworthy enough for agents to act on. Provenance. Every node records who wrote it — which person or which agent — from which source, and when. An answer can then say where it came from, and a reviewer can discount a claim that came from an agent's inference rather than a human decision. In SHIP an agent's write is recorded as an agent observation and audit logged; it does not silently become fact. Supersession. Knowledge changes. A decision that is replaced should not be deleted — the history of why it changed is often the most useful part — but it must be marked as superseded, with a link to what replaced it. Retrieval over documents has no equivalent: the old version and the new one are just two passages. MCP is the boundary The Model Context Protocol gives agents a typed interface to a system: a list of tools, each with a schema. For a knowledge base that is the right boundary, because it makes the contract explicit: Reads are broad: search, fetch a node, traverse its relations. Writes are narrow and attributable: record an observation, propose a status change, link two nodes — never "rewrite the graph". Some writes are not offered at all. Where an agent writing a wrong value is worse than no agent, the tool is read only and the record is still entered by a person. The capability you leave out is part of the design. The same interface serves every assistant the user already has. One knowledge base, reachable from whichever client a person prefers, beats a separate memory locked inside each. When retrieval is still right Typed structure is not free: someone, or something, has to create the nodes. For large bodies of reference text — manuals, regulations, research — retrieval remains the right tool, ideally hybrid and with citations back to the source passage. The practical architecture is both: a typed core for the things the organisation decides and owns, and retrieval around it for the things it reads. The short version Retrieval finds passages; organisations run on decisions. Hybrid search for recall, re ranking for precision, citations for trust. Type the knowledge that changes and matters: goals, decisions, artefacts. Record provenance on every write and supersede rather than delete. Make the agent interface narrow where mistakes are expensive. The harness note covers how this knowledge reaches a model as context, and the agentic workflows note how to check what the model does with it.

For most of the history of software, the expensive part was writing the code. Planning, process and team shape all grew around that constraint. Agents have not removed it, but they have moved it: a competent first draft of a change is now minutes away. What is still slow is knowing which change to make, and knowing whether the one you got is right. That shift changes what good product engineering looks like, and it changes it for product managers and engineering leaders as much as for engineers. The new bottlenecks Used to be scarce Now scarce Typing the code Saying precisely what should change Knowing the syntax Knowing which details decide whether it holds up Review of a colleague's diff Review of a machine's diff, at volume Writing tests Writing checks the author cannot game Documentation nobody reads Briefs an agent reads on every task Every row on the right is a judgement problem. None of them gets easier because the model got better at code. The spec is the artefact When an agent implements, the spec stops being a ticket someone skims and becomes the input that determines the output. A good one is short and specific: What and why — the user problem, in one paragraph. The shape of done — what someone will see, and the check that proves it. Constraints — what must not change, what must not be invented, which existing pattern to follow. Open questions — named, so they get answered rather than guessed. Writing that well is product work. It is also the cheapest point in the whole process to catch a wrong idea — the plan costs a minute to read; the implementation of the wrong plan costs a review cycle and a revert. Taste becomes configuration Every team has standards that live in people's heads: how dense a table should be, which error messages are acceptable, why a figure is never shown without its source, when a number must say it was simulated. Agents do not absorb those by osmosis. They follow what is written down. So taste moves into files: a design system with named components and tokens, a brief per repository, rules that attach to the paths they govern, checks that fail the build when a raw colour sneaks past the tokens. This site is an example — its brief carries rules like never fabricate market data and motion must compute something , and every change, by a person or an agent, starts from them. The side effect is welcome: standards that are written down can be argued with, versioned and improved. Standards in people's heads mostly get re litigated. Verification scales the team If an agent can produce ten changes a day, the team needs to be able to trust ten changes a day. That is a verification problem, and it is solved the same way it always was, only with less tolerance for gaps: fast, strict gates that run on every change; property and invariant tests for anything that computes; a real environment to look at, not just a green build; humans reviewing intent and risk, not formatting. The agentic workflows note goes into the gates. The organisational point is that investment in verification used to be a quality decision. It is now a capacity decision. The product–engineering line moves When implementation is cheap, the person closest to the problem can often get much further on their own. Product managers prototype the change instead of describing it. Engineers spend more time on what to build and how to prove it, and less on transcription. Designers ship the component rather than the picture of it. That does not remove the roles. It removes the hand offs between them that existed only because writing code was slow. What remains distinct is accountability: who decides what good is, and who answers for it when it is not. Knowledge is infrastructure An agent is only as good as what it knows about the product, the codebase and the decisions behind both. A team that keeps its goals, decisions and artefacts somewhere structured — not scattered across chat threads and stale wiki pages — gives every agent and every new hire the same head start. That is the problem SHIP exists for, and the knowledge bases note explains why typed structure beats retrieval for it. What to do on Monday 1. Write a one page brief for your main repository: purpose, hard rules, the command that proves a change works. 2. Make that command fast enough that people — and agents — actually run it. 3. Turn your three most frequent review comments into rules or checks. 4. Require a written plan before any change larger than a single file. 5. Keep irreversible steps — deploys, data changes, messages to customers — behind a human, explicitly. None of it needs a new tool. All of it gets more valuable the more of the work is done by agents.

A short list rather than a long one. Everything here I have actually read, and I have said why in my own words — go to the publishers for the real thing. The reference Options, Futures and Other Derivatives — John C. Hull. The standard text, and standard for a reason: it is the book desks actually keep on the shelf. Not a book to read cover to cover. A book to own and open at the chapter you need, which for most people is binomial trees first and the Greeks second. Option Volatility and Pricing — Sheldon Natenberg. Where Hull gives you the mathematics, Natenberg gives you the trader's intuition for what the numbers mean when the market is moving. If you only read one, and you intend to trade rather than to price, read this one. Dynamic Hedging — Nassim Nicholas Taleb. Difficult, opinionated, and written by someone who ran the risk rather than modelled it. Worth the effort specifically for its treatment of the places where the standard model quietly stops working. Narrative and memoir The textbooks tell you how the instruments work. These tell you what happens when people use them. Liar's Poker — Michael Lewis. Salomon Brothers in the eighties, and more or less the book that invented this genre. Everything below is in conversation with it. The Big Short — Michael Lewis. Sharper than the film on the actual mechanics of the trade: what the CDS contracts said, why the counterparties kept writing them, and how long being right can take. Flash Boys — Michael Lewis. HFT and market microstructure. Contested by practitioners on several points, and still the most readable route into why venue design, latency and order routing decide who gets filled. When Genius Failed — Roger Lowenstein. The definitive account of LTCM: a quant fund with the right models blowing up on a liquidity constraint and a correlated market. The relevant lesson is not that the mathematics was wrong. Fool's Gold — Gillian Tett. The JPMorgan team that invented the credit derivatives later used to blow up the system. Narrative rather than textbook, and unusually good on how a well intentioned instrument gets away from its authors. On risk, more broadly Against the Gods — Peter L. Bernstein. A history of how humanity learned to measure risk at all. Useful perspective on why the tools look the way they do. The Black Swan — Nassim Nicholas Taleb. Overexposed and still worth it, if you read it as an argument about the shape of distributions rather than as general purpose contrarianism. Engineering, for the systems underneath Designing Data Intensive Applications — Martin Kleppmann. Nothing to do with options, everything to do with building the systems that price them. The chapters on consistency and stream processing are the ones that mattered to me when we were building risk engines that had to be correct at a million updates a second. Where else to look The exchange documentation is better than most books for mechanics — specifications, margin methodology, contract terms. It is dry, free, and authoritative, which is a rare combination. If you want to understand SPAN margining, the exchange's own methodology paper will teach you more in an hour than any textbook chapter.

A film has two hours and needs a crisis to fill them. A series has time for the ordinary weeks — the standups, the politics, the slow attrition — which is where almost all of the actual job lives. On the desk Industry (2020– ). The most accurate thing on screen about grad scheme culture, desk politics and the psychological cost of sell side trading. It gets the jargon and the hierarchy right, which almost nothing else does, and it is honest that most of the pressure is social rather than mathematical. On the buy side Billions (2016–2023). Hedge fund against US Attorney, at length. More about power and ego than mechanics, but genuinely good on activist positions, the politics of a fund's investor base, and the grey edges of insider trading. Adjacent, and worth it Succession (2018–2023). Not finance exactly, and still essential on family controlled conglomerates, M&A, and how a board actually gets worked. If you have ever sat in a governance meeting where the real decision happened somewhere else, it will feel familiar. Watch all three for the culture rather than the mechanics. None of them will teach you to price anything, and that is not what they are for.

Watch these for the culture, not the mechanics — all of them compress and simplify, and some of them are fiction throughout. Ranked roughly by how much of the job they get right. The ones that get it right Margin Call (2011). The best of them: a risk model returns an unacceptable number overnight, and the rest is people deciding what to do about it. Understated, dialogue driven, and accurate about hierarchy in a way the others are not. If you watch one, watch this. The Big Short (2015). The clearest popular explanation of CDOs and credit default swaps ever put on screen, at the cost of some caricature. Conceptually sound, and the fourth wall explainers earn their place. Read the book for the mechanics. Trading Places (1983). A comedy that ends in a commodities pit, and genuinely useful on how a corner works. Also responsible, indirectly, for a rule in US law about trading on misappropriated government data. The ones about the culture Wall Street (1987) and Money Never Sleeps (2010). Dated, and still the cultural template for the whole era — "greed is good" came from here, and was not meant as advice. Watch the first; the sequel is for completeness. Boiler Room (2000). Pump and dump brokerage culture. More about sales cults than about trading, which is precisely what makes it useful: the pressure it depicts is real and has not gone anywhere. The Wolf of Wall Street (2013). Stratton Oakmont at full volume. About excess and fraud rather than markets. Enjoyable, frequently mistaken for aspirational, and worth watching only if you keep that straight.
